description_full: AutoZone, Inc. operates as a retailer and distributor of automotive replacement parts and accessories in the Americas. The company offers a product line for cars, sport utility vehicles, vans, and light duty trucks, including new and remanufactured automotive hard parts, maintenance items, accessories, and non-automotive products. It also provides failure products, such as A/C compressors, batteries and accessories, bearings, belts and hoses, calipers, chassis, clutches, CV axles, engines, fuel pumps, fuses, ignition, lighting, mufflers, radiators, starters and alternators, thermostats, tire repair, and water pumps. In addition, the company offers maintenance products, including antifreeze and windshield washer fluid; brake drums, rotors, shoes, and pads; chemicals, including brake and power steering fluid, and oil and fuel additives; oil and transmission fluid; oil, cabin, air, fuel, and transmission filters; oxygen sensors; paint and accessories; refrigerant and accessories; shock absorbers and struts; spark plugs and wires; and windshield wipers. Further, it provides air fresheners, cell phone accessories, drinks and snacks, floor mats and seat covers, interior and exterior accessories, mirrors, performance products protectants and cleaners, sealants and adhesives, steering wheel covers, tools, towing, vehicle entertainment systems, and wash and wax. It offers its products under the AutoZone, AutoZone Rewards, Get in the Zone, Zone, Duralast, Econocraft, ProElite, ProVantage, ShopPro, SureBilt, TotalPro, TruGrade, Valucraft, and ALLDATA names. The company sells its products through stores, www.autozone.com, www.autozonepro.com, www.alldata.com, and www.duralastparts.com, as well as commercial sales program that provides delivery of parts and other products and commercial credit to local, regional and national repair garages, dealers, service stations, fleet owners, and other accounts. AutoZone, Inc. was founded in 1979 and is headquartered in Memphis, Tennessee.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 79K people. Revenue per employee of $257K ranks in the below the sector median among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 7%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $23K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 11× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: AutoZone, Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $51.8B market cap on $20.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 86% against a 7% cost of capital — a 79-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 52% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.8B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.26× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 2.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 7.6×.

Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 11pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.22x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+7.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 21% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 8% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 20% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 0.62, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $764.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 39% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 37% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 5% below its DCF fair value of $3,391, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 2%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $2,315 to $5,084 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: EV/EBITDA 15.4 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 28.5 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 42% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $3,666 on average, 14% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 86% clears the cost of capital of 7.4% by 79pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.36).
It runs a 52% gross margin and converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.26x.
It spends 0.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.0x net debt to EBITDA ($326.1M of cash against $9.1B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 7.6x.
The current ratio of 0.90 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.2% over 3 years, 6.8% over 5 years and 6.7% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 31% of profits supports about 27.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -8.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 2.1x depreciation (7.0% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 12.9% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 99%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 21 sales over the past year, net $27.1M sold.
It returns 3.9% a year to shareholders (3.9% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 10.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 79,200 employees, each generates about $257K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 6.6% a year.
That works out to $23K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.9M (11x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
